data.title: 80% of workers make this 401(k) mistake when they retire
data.description:
By Beth Pinsker

Tax repercussions crop up down the road as balances build up, and RMDs get complicated

When faced with too many choices in retirement, many retirees do nothing instead.

What's the first thing most people do with their 401(k) after they retire? Nothing.

That's the finding of a new Vanguard report, "How America Retires 2026," which documents current retiree behavior based on the large population in its orbit of the 401(k) plans the company administers, much like Vanguard's yearly landmark "How America Saves" study.

In particular, researchers dug deep into the accounts of 160,000 former employees in company 401(k) plans administered by Vanguard who were 60 or older and had account balances over $100,000. The balance minimum was selected because these would be people who weren't cashed out automatically for having a low balance, and would be presumed to have some engagement with their accounts. "Retirees at this balance level are more likely to make ongoing decisions about asset allocation, withdrawals, rollovers and retirement income," the report said.

The surprising finding was that 80% of the group that was 60 to 72 - thus before required minimum distributions kicked in - did not touch their accounts in the year after they retired. Some 15% took occasional withdrawals, while 7% took regular installment distributions.

The study was able to look at successive years of behavior, too. The trends continued for about three years, with more retirees rolling over their accounts each year. But still, a significant number of retirees stayed in the plans and left their money alone. For 2021 retirees, for instance, 55% stayed in the plan, while about 9% cashed out in some fashion and 36% rolled over their accounts to an IRA or another 401(k) at a new employer. Two years later, only 34% were still in the plan, 50% had rolled over and 16% had cashed out.

What matters about this is the stagnation. While it might seem like it's good that most retirees are not spending or moving their money around, there are actually financial repercussions to this.

One danger noted in a new study on "retirement drift," by Empower, one of the biggest retirement-plan administrators, found that one in three workers have lost track of old retirement plans. People want to "set it and forget it," but then they actually do forget it. This is another reason why Vanguard focused on accounts with $100,000 or more, reasoning that people would be less likely to forget a high balance.

RMD confusion

Vanguard also found that the lack of interaction between people and their accounts seems to be because of confusion about required minimum distributions (RMDs). Nearly half of retirees misunderstood the rule to mean that they shouldn't take money until RMD age - which for those included in the study was 73, but is 75 for those born 1960 and later. People also think that they are only supposed to take the RMD amount, which is actually a very conservative percentage of the prior year's balance.

If you wait until 73 or 75 to take RMDs and then only take the required amount, you will likely end up with a higher balance at the end of your life than you started with at the beginning of retirement. People who follow this path also likely take Social Security at the earliest point, age 62, permanently lowering their benefit amount. Financial advisers say that most retirees benefit from waiting until full retirement age, which is now 67, or until the maximum benefit age of 70, to start Social Security and should withdraw money from tax-deferred accounts to cover living expenses instead.

For high-balance accounts, steady withdrawals starting early can also mitigate some of the tax impact of large RMDs. If you retire at 65, for instance, and don't start taking RMDs until 75, your account could grow significantly in 10 years, raising that RMD high enough to push you over the limit for Medicare fees known as IRMAA and increasing the taxation of your Social Security income.

Vanguard's answer for this is more education, firmly pressing employers to adopt 401(k) plan designs that are more flexible in retirement and to provide participants with more information.

"The research also shows that plan design matters, with recent retirees more than 40% more likely to remain in their workplace plan when flexible withdrawal options such as partial withdrawals and installment payments are available," said Jeff Clark, Vanguard's head of defined contribution research, in a statement to MarketWatch.

Not a silver bullet

From the data, it might seem like the real problem is people leaving their funds in their 401(k) plans to stagnate, and then potentially forgetting them. But it's not necessarily a magic fix to just get more people to roll over their 401(k)s to IRAs in retirement.

Other Vanguard research finds that many people leave IRA accounts in cash, rather than investing the funds, and that could severely affect account growth. Cash, especially if the money is swept into non-interest or low-interest bearing accounts, is not likely to keep up with inflation. The money would have to be in a government money-market account or other high-yield savings vehicle to even have a chance.

But many people misunderstand the vital difference between a 401(k) and an IRA. In the workplace plan, you can really set it and forget it, because employees are now likely to be auto-enrolled into a target-date fund or other managed portfolio that will adjust for risk as they age. Even if an employee did take an interest and pick their own investments, they'd have only about 15-30 choices of mutual funds, most of which would align to broad-market indexes or sectors.

In an IRA, you have to invest the funds yourself, and there are thousands to choose from. Behavioral finance has long found that people get analysis paralysis after about 30 options.

Vanguard research, as well as that from Fidelity and others, had found that people don't understand that there are multiple steps to the process - roll over the funds, then invest them, then manage them as you go forward. Others get that, but then get overwhelmed by the choices and never come back to select funds once the rollover cash settles.

Education, again, is one solution for this, but there are opportunities for better plan design. IRA custodians can better nudge people to make investing decisions and help them through the process. They can also make "in-kind" transfers more of an option, which means the investments from the 401(k) transfer over exactly the same, rather than being liquidated to cash as the default.

"One of the clearest findings from 'How America Retires' is that there is no single path people follow once they retire," Clark said.

That means there isn't one single solution to make things better, but rather many things to work on for the future.

data.title: We're in our 70s. Should we pay off our 2.5% mortgage - or put the money in a high-yield savings account?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'Let's say 10 years from now, when I'm 84, we need a substantial amount of cash'

"Instead of making extra mortgage payments, we've decided to put that exact same money into a high-yield savings account." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

We're a retired couple living in Southern California. I'm 74, and my wife is 70. We are weighing up the wisdom of investing in a market driven by artificial intelligence and deciding whether to instead keep money in cash or pay off our mortgage.

I enjoyed your article about the couple with the mortgage (We have a $300,000 mortgage with a 2.75% interest rate. I want to pay it off. My husband says I'm crazy. Who's right?).

Our mortgage carries a slightly lower interest rate (2.5%) than the one in that story, and my original plan was to make extra payments and pay it off in 15 years.

But then I started asking myself a different question: If we need access to cash at some point in the future, where is that money better off - in home equity or in the bank?

Let's say that 10 years from now, when I'm 84, we need a substantial amount of cash. At that point, would I rather have the money tied up in the house or available when we need it?

So instead of making extra mortgage payments, we've decided to put that exact same money into a high-yield savings account and, as the balance grows, build a CD ladder.

As I see it, there are two primary benefits and a possible third one as well:

-- Liquidity over home equity. I'd rather have cash in hand than money tied up in the house. In other words, a bird in the hand is worth two in the bush - especially as we get older and having readily available funds becomes increasingly important.

-- An added layer of title protection. Keeping a mortgage with an established lender may offer some additional safeguards, although it's not a substitute for independent title monitoring or other protective measures.

-- A potential tax benefit. Mortgage interest may still be tax-deductible. However, with the standard deduction, that benefit may be limited or nonexistent for many homeowners.

I'm simply suggesting that, particularly in retirement, having accessible cash and maintaining financial flexibility may be worth more than paying off the mortgage early.

What do you think?

Homeowner in my 70s in Temecula

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Related: My wife never went back to work after raising our kids. Do I have to share my retirement savings 50/50?

Given your favorable situation, especially with your low interest rate, there's no right or wrong decision.

Dear Homeowner,

You're in the home stretch with your financial journey, and I sure hope you are enjoying it.

With a 2.5% rate on your mortgage, you'll still be ahead if you put your money into a high-yield savings account or CDs. By all means, have an emergency fund, preferably a year's worth of expenses, but please try not to keep a large sum of money in a checking account, because inflation will eat away at that cash over time. Remember, too, that you can buy title insurance with or without a mortgage, and that a lender will always keep its own financial interests at heart.

Given your low interest rate, there's no right or wrong decision. You can get CD rates of 4.5% and HYSA rates of up to 4.25%. That's marginally above the latest consumer price index rate of 3.7%. So you'd be more or less treading water between your returns and inflation with your money stashed in cash equivalents. How much of your excess cash you put in cash or bonds versus the stock market depends on your risk tolerance and purchasing power.

With such a low mortgage rate, there's nothing inherently wrong with paying off your mortgage while building your savings, provided your returns after taxes and other costs justify it. A well-structured CD ladder, in addition to other more readily available sources, is also a good idea. This would allow you to meet unexpected expenses without having to sell investments during a market downturn or, perish the thought, borrow against your home.

Having faith in the market

When you're in your 70s, financial advisers generally recommend you have 30% to 50% of your portfolio in bonds or cash equivalents, and the rest in stocks. The idea is to avoid being held hostage by a major market correction or, worse, a recession by being forced to withdraw money during a down market. But plenty of people in your age group dance to the beat of their own financial drum and have 70% or more in stock while relying on Social Security and other forms of income.

The S&P 500 SPX, Dow Jones Industrial Average DJIA and Nasdaq Composite Index (COMP) have all been on an upward trajectory this year. The Nasdaq has benefited from the AI gold rush. If you have faith in the long-term future of U.S. equities, as history would suggest you might, you could invest in an exchange-traded fund that tracks the total market, the S&P 500 or some other diversified index, perhaps a Vanguard Total Stock Market ETF VTI.

In October, Yardeni Research published a research note cautioning that the yield on the 2-year Treasury note had risen 115 basis points from its December low, indicating higher borrowing costs that could put pressure on stock valuations. However, Yardeni analysts also noted that credit conditions outside the AI sector do not yet show the widespread excessive lending that preceded some prior market downturns (which is not quite a confidence booster).

The International Monetary Fund, also in October, warned that global financial markets face elevated risks from an AI-driven market correction if the billions of dollars being spent on AI don't generate the expected economic returns. "Three key risks have been increasing, each with the potential for broader implications: an artificial intelligence-driven market correction, a sharper rise in sovereign bond yields, and cyberattacks," the IMF said.

Mulling over safer havens

For other safe havens, consider shorter-duration bonds or mutual funds and exchange-traded funds that invest in bonds with maturities of less than five years, as well as Treasury inflation-protected securities (TIPS), which are inflation-protected bonds issued by the U.S. Treasury. Some analysts also see upside in value-oriented and defensive sectors, including consumer staples, utilities and healthcare stocks, for retired investors who seek safety over higher returns.

Ultimately, your investment strategy in retirement will depend on your lifestyle, how much money you have in your retirement-account balances, your goals, your views on the current socioeconomic backdrop and, yes, whether you think the tech boom will continue unabated (there is no consensus on that). Do you have long-term-care insurance or life insurance? How much longer do you have to pay on your mortgage? Will your passive income in retirement continue to cover your expenses?

The question you ask is timely because you can't answer it in isolation. It forces you to step back and look at your entire retirement plan. Are you, for example, comfortable withdrawing 4% from your retirement accounts in the first year and adjusting that rate for inflation in subsequent years? How much of your retirement savings are in traditional accounts versus Roth accounts? And, yes, how big are your mortgage payments? Do they account for more than 30% of your monthly income?

Once you answer these many questions, you can make your decision with relative ease.

data.title: Want guaranteed income in retirement without an annuity? Try laddering I bonds.
data.description:
By Beth Pinsker

How to use I-bonds to create inflation-proof income in retirement

Your retirement savings need to keep up with inflation, and Series I bonds are designed to do just that.

The interest rates for Series I bonds reset every six months, on Nov. 1 and May 1, and at times when inflation is rising, these announcements become news events. However, if you're using I-bonds the way they were intended, as an inflation hedge, it shouldn't matter that much to you. Each year, no matter what, you'd be buying a set dollar amount - up to the $10,000-a-year limit for each Social Security number - and then letting it ride.

That's what Scott Cederburg has been doing for the past five years, in a very tortoiselike approach that he calls setting up his own "retirement annuity." It actually goes against his nature: Cederburg is a 44-year-old professor of finance at the Eller College of Management at the University of Arizona, and his best-known piece of research involves putting 100% of a retirement portfolio into stocks. He not only studies this, he also practices it with his own retirement funds, which are split between U.S. and international funds.

"All of my retirement is 100% equity," said Cederburg. "I think of the I-bonds as a supplement to Social Security. That's real income."

His game plan is to keep putting away $10,000 a year in I-bonds for the next 20 or so years, until retirement. He buys the bonds from TreasuryDirect.gov once a year, a 10-minute task he doesn't think about again until it's time to buy again the next year. When he started this process in 2021, the fixed rate on I-bonds was 0% and the inflation rate was minimal. He wasn't making much in terms of interest, but he wasn't losing ground, either.

For the rate that lasts through Oct. 31, the fixed part is 0.90% and the annualized adjustable inflation rate is 3.34%, for a combined six-month rate of 4.26%. TipsWatch.com, a website from journalist David Enna that closely watches rates on Treasury products, predicts the rate announced for Nov. 1 will be a fixed rate of 1.4% and an inflation rate of 4.08%, for an annualized combined rate of 5.51%. If the fixed rate is 1.3% instead, the annualized combined rate would be 5.41%, Enna noted.

Either way, that rate is attractive compared with all the other options on the market right now, like CDs, high-yield savings accounts or short-term Treasurys.

But that's beside the point, really. The strategy for I-bonds is a long-term one. It's an inflation hedge for savings, not a way to chase yields. And that's exactly why Cederburg compares it to an annuity and doesn't even consider it part of his investing portfolio, which is invested quite aggressively.

The endgame with I-bonds

What matters most about I-bonds, if you save consistently over the years, is how you plan on withdrawing the money. Cederburg does not have a spreadsheet or software to plan out this process. He keeps it very simple: right now the money is going in, and later he will start taking it out. What he likes about I-bonds versus, say Treasury inflation-protected securities, is that you don't have to worry about redeeming at a particular maturity date.

If you buy TIPS directly from the government, you have to buy them in durations of 5, 10 or 30 years. If you buy maturity-based exchange-traded funds, you can build a ladder of the intervening years, but that means that each year, you have to commit to a certain amount coming due. The same goes for CDs or Treasury bills, bonds and notes, which don't have built-in inflation protection but do have maturity terms.

You can cash in I-bonds once you pass the one-year maturity lock-in. If you sell within five years, you lose three months of interest payments, but after five years, you are free to cash them in at any point at full value plus growth. You can also choose which I-bonds you cash in, so you have a lot of control. They reach full maturity after 30 years, after which they no longer earn interest. You pay federal ordinary income taxes on the interest upon redemption, but that interest is exempt from state and local income taxes.

"Once you get into retirement, you can choose which I-bonds to take out," said Cederburg. "At that point, it's optimal to take out the ones with the lowest rate. I have some at a zero percent fixed rate. I'd take those out first. If they raise the fixed rate on Nov. 1, that might be a bond that I hold onto longer."

Cederburg locked onto I-bonds because he was studying inflation and found I-bonds to be the best option for fixed-income savings. They beat TIPS for simplicity, ease of use, taxation and sometimes on rates. They also beat annuities on inflation protection. "Some annuities are suited to protect you from longevity risk, but a lot of annuities are not inflation protected. You get a set dollar amount a year, but it doesn't guarantee you buying power with that," he said.

While $10,000 may not sound like an enormous amount of retirement savings, it will add up over time. If Cederburg maintains this strategy for 25 years, he'll have $250,000 in principal, plus growth that equals the inflation rate. He has assured purchasing power. He can then start taking out money. If he ends up with a balance of around $400,000 at age 65, he could create an income stream for 30 years that is around $2,000 a month.

Not bad for 10 minutes of work a year. "From my perspective, that's the nice thing about it. Set it once and forget it, and come back 20 years later," Cederburg said.

data.title: Our church has a $1.5 million bequest earning 3.75% in a savings account. Are we throwing money away?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'Given the size and long-term nature of this gift, we want to make sure the funds are managed prudently'

"Our concern is that this rate of return may barely keep pace with inflation." (Photo subjects are models.)

Dear Quentin,

A Catholic church in central Massachusetts recently received a $1.5 million bequest from a generous parishioner who has passed away. Under the current arrangement, the bank holding the funds will distribute 4% annually for 25 years.

We understand that the funds are currently invested in a savings account earning 3.75%. Our concern is that this may barely keep pace with inflation, and there may be better investment options available to the church.

We would greatly appreciate your thoughts and insights on several questions:

-- How should the church consider investing these assets to balance growth, preservation of principal and the need for annual distributions? Should the church require the bank to enter into a formal fiduciary agreement, and what protections would that provide?

-- Would it be preferable for the bank to distribute the funds quarterly, semiannually or annually? What are the potential risks and advantages of having the bank continue to manage the funds compared with engaging another financial institution or investment management company?

-- Should the church arrange for periodic independent financial audits of the fund? Would it be advisable for the church to retain a CPA, financial adviser, or investment professional to provide independent oversight?

Given the size and long-term nature of this gift, we want to make sure the funds are managed prudently and in the best interests of the parish and its future parishioners.

A Parishioner

Don't miss: 'My main goal is to help people': I'm single, 74, with $10 million burning a hole in my pocket. What should I do?

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

No doubt this gift has raised a lot of questions, not least how to spend it.

Dear Parishoner,

Your church must have provided that parishioner with a great sense of community and spiritual healing to inspire such a generous gift.

No doubt it has raised a lot of questions, not least how to spend it. If that $1.5 million was put in a trust with instructions on how it should be distributed and invested over time, your church - as the beneficiary - may have less control over the interest rate. That would be up to the trustee. If, however, the money was given outright and the trustee are board members of your church, that's a different story. But you are correct: the consumer price index hit 3.7% in September.

A 3.75% interest rate is not a bad rate for a certificate of deposit (CD) or high-yield savings account, and slightly below what you might get for a 1-year Treasury bill. For a gift such as this, the church board or trustee is likely to prioritize safety over returns. Brian Katz, chief investment officer at Prosperity Wealth Management, agrees that 3.75% is a competitive rate. "The real question, which can only be answered by the church's decision makers, is how much risk they are willing to take," he told me.

"Given the long time horizon of 25 years and the relatively low disbursement rate of 4%, the portfolio has the leeway to take on more risk," he says. "One idea for a little higher yield without adding too much incremental risk would be an ultrashort bond fund. These can be found in both ETF and mutual fund structures. Currently, you can likely find something that yields 4.0% to 4.25%. As I said before, given the time horizon, building a diversified portfolio that includes equities, bonds, and cash may be considered, depending on the church's risk tolerance."

Don't miss: I'm a single 58-year-old veteran in California with $1.5 million and a VA pension. Can I retire?

Stock-market exposure

There's probably room for some stock-market exposure. "A conservative allocation of 20% equities and 80% bonds and cash wouldn't expose the portfolio to too much risk and should allow for a modestly higher return profile," Katz adds. "By focusing your equity investments on funds that favor high-quality or dividend-paying equities, the church could reduce the risk of the overall portfolio. The bond portfolio could include funds that purchase short-to-intermediate-term bonds, which would offset some of the duration risk."

The timing of distributions, if you have control over it, depends on how the church's finances are structured, but the longer you leave the money invested, the better the potential return. "The question on timing of the distributions should be made in consideration of the church's operating budget," Katz says. "From an investment standpoint, the longer the money remains invested, the more the investor benefits from compounding returns. Therefore, taking it out once at the end of the year can maximize the expected return of the portfolio."

You may also decide to use some of this money as an emergency fund, in case the church needs to replace the roof or - if you carry out broader renovations - is required to upgrade the entranceway or access to the restrooms to meet city standards. "The church should have an investment committee and a charter that defines the committee's roles and responsibilities," Katz adds. "Hiring an adviser is not a bad idea." In principle, a trust can be structured so that part of the investment income is distributed to a church while another part is reinvested.

It all depends on how the $1.5 million is held, who controls it, and what restrictions govern its use.

data.title: What gave this city its 'best place to retire' crown? You can actually afford to live there.
data.description:
By Jessica Hall

This Midwestern city came in first for the second year in a row

Someone turning 65 today can expect to live nearly two more decades, meaning Americans need to carefully select where to retire.

The cost of living is top of mind for Americans of all ages, cementing Midland, Mich., as the best place to retire for the second year in a row.

The Midwestern city of about 42,500 people held on to its top spot due to its low cost of living, high quality of life and favorable retiree taxes, according to the latest ranking by U.S. News & World Report.

"The whole country is feeling the pinch right now, so it's not a surprise that affordability is a top priority," Megan Wood, managing editor of home services and real estate at U.S. News, told MarketWatch.

Midland's affordability metrics looked at items such as the cost of shelter, including rents and mortgages, as well as utilities, transportation and fuel and consumer goods and services. The city does not impose a local sales or income tax, and Michigan does not tax Social Security income.

Last year, Midland nabbed the top spot due to quality of life, as well as affordability. Its top ranking this year was driven by affordability. Midland's community is active, with abundant senior programming for social and cultural events, as well as many options for senior housing, Wood said. About 23% of its residents are over the age of 45 and 20% are over age 65.

The city, which is about two hours from Detroit and near Lake Huron's Saginaw Bay, is the headquarters of chemical company Dow (DOW). In addition to its thriving arts and cultural scene, Midland is known for an abundance of midcentury modern architecture. It's also home to the minor league baseball team the Great Lakes Loons.

"Retirees are seeking a place that gives them a sense of security and comfort as they live out their golden years," Wood said. "Whether that comfort prioritizes scenic nature spots, access to multicultural experiences, or everyday affordability, places like Midland, Michigan, offer financial safety while still providing a good quality of life."

U.S. News adjusted its scoring weights for the new rankings to mirror growing concerns over affordability in the United States. This resulted in multiple double-digit jumps among the top 25, including No. 8 Paducah, Ky., landing in the top 10 for the first time.

The report comes as roughly 18% of the U.S. population is now 65 or older. An adult turning 65 today can expect to live nearly two more decades, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. That puts increased importance on the decision about where to retire, since retirement itself could last decades.

More than one in three retirees have moved during retirement, according to 2025 research by the nonprofit Transamerica Institute and the Transamerica Center for Retirement Studies. Among those who moved, the top reasons included being closer to family and friends, downsizing into a smaller home, starting a new chapter in life, reducing expenses, moving to a place with a better climate and no longer needing to live near work, Transamerica found.

Midland is followed on the list by Homosassa Springs, Fla., which is bolstered by its strong affordability scores, growth of its older population and low retiree taxes. Weirton, W. Va., came in at No. 3 with high marks for quality of life, low retiree taxes, affordability and quality of life.

Traditional retiree hotspots such as Florida and Texas each appeared twice in the top 10 and multiple times throughout the listing of the top 250 locales, while states such as California and New Jersey fell toward the bottom of the list due to their high cost of living, Wood said.

U.S. News evaluated more than 850 U.S. cities based on how well they meet American retirees' expectations against measures including quality of life, affordability, healthcare, retiree taxes, job market, and population and migration for retirees ages 55 and older.

"This ranking is meant to be used as a starting point for retirees to do more research and find the best place that suits them," Wood said.

Other rankings of the best places to retire earlier this year highlighted Florida, with Orlando taking the top spot in WalletHub's recent study due to favorable taxes and access to quality healthcare. Meanwhile, Wyoming topped a report by CareScout, a company that helps families find eldercare, due to the state's lack of personal income tax and its having lowest rate in the nation of multiple chronic conditions among Medicare beneficiaries.

-Jessica Hall

RADNOR, Pa., Oct. 31, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Kessler Topaz Meltzer & Check, LLP (www.ktmc.com), a nationally recognized securities litigation law firm, informs investors that a securities fraud class action lawsuit has been filed against Fluence Energy, Inc. (Fluence Energy) (NASDAQ: FLNC) on behalf of those who purchased or acquired Fluence Energy securities between November 24, 2025 and September 16, 2026, inclusive. The lawsuit is filed in the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York and is captioned Hatweek v. Fluence Energy, Inc., No. 1:26-cv-08475 (S.D.N.Y.).  Investors have until November 27, 2026, to file for lead plaintiff status. 

CONTACT KTMC TO DISCUSS YOUR LEGAL RIGHTS:    
If you purchased or acquired Fluence Energy securities and have lost money on your investment, please provide your information here: https://www.ktmc.com/flnc-fluence-energy-inc-class-action-lawsuit?utm_source=PR_Newswire&utm_medium=pressrelease&utm_campaign=flnc&mktm=PR 

You can also contact attorney Jonathan Naji, Esq. by calling (484) 270-1453 or by email at info@ktmc.com.  There is no cost or obligation to speak with an attorney.

To view the Fluence Energy video on YouTube, click here: https://youtu.be/Hmn8AUJTqQQ 

FLUENCE ENERGY, INC. CLASS ACTION LAWSUIT - COMPLAINT ALLEGATION SUMMARY:
The complaint alleges that, throughout the Class Period, Defendants made materially false and/or misleading statements, as well as failed to disclose material facts about the company's business, operations, and prospects. Specifically, Defendants misrepresented and/or failed to disclose that: (1) Fluence Energy's ability to deliver its backlog and recognize the revenue underlying its fiscal 2026 guidance depended on new contract manufacturing facilities, including facilities that were not completed, not operational, and/or not capable of producing at the volumes the company's guidance assumed; (2) the corrective measures Fluence Energy had implemented to address production problems at its contract manufacturers were not resolving those problems, which continued and extended to the company's new facilities; and (3) as a result of the foregoing, Defendants' statements about the company's business, operations, and prospects were materially false and misleading and/or lacked a reasonable basis at all relevant times.

Why did Fluence Energy's Stock Drop?
On February 4, 2026 and August 5, 2026, Fluence Energy reported disappointing quarterly financial results, including GAAP gross profit margin declines, an increase in net losses, and weaker than expected revenue.  As a result, Fluence Energy's stock price fell significantly and the company slashed its fiscal year 2026 revenue guidance and its adjusted EBITDA guidance.

Then, on September 16, 2026, Fluence Energy announced through a mid-quarter guidance update that the company was cutting its full year revenue guidance by approximately $600 million to $2.4 billion. Additionally, Fluence Energy further cut its full year adjusted EBITDA guidance from negative $10 million to negative $200 million, attributed to "delays in the ramp-up of our contract manufacturing facility."  On this news, Fluence Energy's stock price fell $1.39 per share, or 15.36%, to close at $7.66 per share on September 17, 2026.

WHAT FLUENCE ENERGY, INC. INVESTORS CAN DO NOW:

  1. File to be lead plaintiff by November 27, 2026.
  2. Contact KTMC for a free case evaluation. All representation is on a contingency fee basis, there is no cost to you.
  3. Retain counsel of choice or take no action.

THE LEAD PLAINTIFF PROCESS FOR FLUENCE ENERGY, INC. INVESTORS:
Fluence Energy investors may, no later than November 27, 2026, seek to be appointed as a lead plaintiff representative of the class through Kessler Topaz Meltzer & Check, LLP or other counsel, or may choose to do nothing and remain an absent class member. A lead plaintiff is a representative party who acts on behalf of all class members in directing the litigation.  The lead plaintiff is usually the investor or small group of investors who have the largest financial interest and who are also adequate and typical of the proposed class of investors. The lead plaintiff selects counsel to represent the lead plaintiff and the class and these attorneys, if approved by the court, are lead or class counsel. Your ability to share in any recovery is not affected by the decision of whether or not to serve as a lead plaintiff.

Kessler Topaz Meltzer & Check, LLP encourages Fluence Energy investors to contact the firm for more information.

Kessler Topaz Meltzer & Check, LLP (KTMC) is a leading U.S. plaintiff-side law firm focused on securities-fraud class actions and global investor protection. The firm represents individual investors as well as institutions, such as major pension funds, asset managers, and international investors.
